title: India Expands Air Cargo Transshipment Network, Targets 80% Growth on Key Routes
excerpt: After a successful pilot on the Chennai-Delhi-Frankfurt corridor that cut transit times from 60 to 20 hours, India adds six new gateways including routes to London and Copenhagen.
body:
• India has expanded its domestic-to-international cargo transshipment network after a successful proof of concept on the Chennai-Delhi-Frankfurt route operated by Air India.
  • The pilot, launched on June 20, transshipped 280 metric tonnes of cargo and pushed aircraft capacity utilisation from 75% to nearly 100%.
  • Four domestic stations (Bengaluru, Ahmedabad, Mumbai, Hyderabad) and two international destinations (London, Copenhagen) have been added to the network.
  • Monthly cargo volumes on these routes are projected to grow from 1,763 tonnes to 3,183 tonnes — an increase of nearly 80%.

India took a significant step toward its ambition of becoming a global air cargo hub this week, as Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu inaugurated the expanded phase of the country's transshipment cargo reforms at Delhi's IGI Airport.

The Chennai-Delhi-Frankfurt Breakthrough

The expansion follows a proof of concept that launched on June 20 on the Chennai-Delhi-Frankfurt sector, with Air India operating the service end-to-end through the Transshipment Excellence Centre at Delhi's Terminal 2.

The results were striking. By eliminating the mandatory re-screening of cargo during transfer — a long-standing bottleneck identified through industry feedback — average end-to-end transit time dropped from 60 hours to just 20 hours. Since launch, the pilot has transshipped 280 metric tonnes of cargo, with aircraft capacity utilisation rising from 75% to nearly 100%.

Six New Gateways

Based on the pilot's success, the network has been expanded to four additional domestic origin stations — Bengaluru, Ahmedabad, Mumbai and Hyderabad — and two new international destinations, London and Copenhagen. The expanded network is projected to increase Air India's monthly cargo carriage on these routes from 1,763 tonnes to 3,183 tonnes, representing nearly 80% growth.

"While our immediate focus is on domestic-to-international transshipment, our larger ambition is to position India as a global cargo transshipment hub by leveraging our strategic location between the East and the West."

— Ram Mohan Naidu, Union Minister for Civil Aviation

Why It Matters for Trade and the Diaspora

The reform addresses a structural disadvantage that has long pushed Indian exporters toward cargo hubs in Dubai, Singapore and Hong Kong. By streamlining transfers at Delhi, India can capture cargo flows that previously routed through competing hubs.

For the Indian diaspora, the expansion has practical implications. Faster and more efficient cargo connectivity between major Indian cities and destinations like Frankfurt, London and Copenhagen could improve delivery times for shipments between India and key diaspora markets in Europe. The addition of Bengaluru, Mumbai and Hyderabad as origin stations is particularly relevant, given the concentration of technology and pharmaceutical exports from these cities.

Chennai's emergence as a key node is notable. The city has recorded the fastest cargo growth among India's top five airports — 16.4% between January and April 2026 — driven by electronics and telecom manufacturing under the government's Production-Linked Incentive schemes.

The government plans to extend the framework to international-to-international and international-to-domestic transshipment, aiming for India to handle 10 million tonnes of air cargo annually by 2030, up from 3.96 million tonnes in FY26.
